The GitHub repository includes documentation, example configurations, and a permissive license that encourages further contributions.

With its initial reception, the Website Wizard is poised to become a useful addition to the JOSM ecosystem, offering map editors a quick path from data to web presentation. The active discussion on Hacker News suggests that the plugin will likely see continued development and refinement as users share use cases and suggest enhancements.
author: Hacker News

title: Anthropic CEO Calls for Slowing AI Development
content:
Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, has announced that the company will begin to slow the pace of its AI development and will grant third‑party evaluators, such as METR, broad access to its models. The move is intended to reinforce the company’s commitment to safety practices and to allow independent verification of its compliance with internal and external standards.

Amodei outlined a three‑step plan to “pace the frontier.” The first step, already underway, is the unilateral provision of model access to external reviewers. The second step calls for industry‑wide cooperation, likely involving government partners, to establish common safety benchmarks and oversight mechanisms. While the final step is not detailed in the brief, it is implied to involve further regulatory alignment and coordinated risk mitigation across the sector.

By opening its models to independent scrutiny, Anthropic aims to create a more transparent development cycle and to give regulators the information needed to assess potential risks. The company’s initiative reflects a growing trend among AI firms to prioritize safety and oversight as they scale up model capabilities. For more detail, see the full story on The Verge.
author: The Verge

title: Sylvan Esso releases new album Ow &∞ and gears up for upcoming event
content:
Sylvan Esso – the electronic‑pop duo of Amelia Meath and Nick Sanborn – announced they will attend the upcoming Frutiger Aero Renfaire, a gathering that blends music, art and retro‑futurist culture. The appearance follows the release of their latest album, Ow &∞, which dropped on Friday and marks the most pronounced stylistic shift in the pair’s catalog to date. The group’s participation in the event was confirmed through a statement released by their publicist, noting that the duo will perform a set featuring selections from the new record alongside earlier material.

Since their debut in 2014 with the self‑titled album and the single “Hey Mami,” Sylvan Esso has issued a series of critically acclaimed releases, including the texturally sparse Free Love (2020) and the rhythm‑driven, glitch‑inflected No Rules Sandy (2022). Their evolving sound has consistently retained the distinctive blend of melodic songwriting and electronic production that defines their work. Ow &∞ expands this foundation with bolder arrangements and experimental tones, signaling a continued commitment to artistic reinvention. The Verge’s full coverage provides additional insight into the album’s composition and the duo’s upcoming plans.
author: The Verge

title: Silicon Valley executives skeptical of recent AI danger warnings
content:
Recent high‑profile warnings about the potential risks of artificial intelligence have sparked a notable degree of scepticism among corporate leaders and venture‑capital investors. Prominent voices—including former government officials, academic researchers, and industry watchdogs—have highlighted concerns ranging from algorithmic bias and privacy breaches to the possibility of autonomous systems acting beyond human control. Their statements have been amplified through media outlets and policy briefings, prompting calls for tighter regulation and more rigorous safety testing before wider deployment.

Executives at leading technology firms and investors in AI‑focused startups, however, have largely questioned the immediacy and severity of these threats. In recent earnings calls and industry conferences, CEOs emphasized ongoing internal risk‑assessment frameworks and the economic benefits of accelerated AI adoption, while venture capitalists cited robust market demand and competitive pressures as drivers for continued funding. The divergence underscores a broader debate over how to balance innovation with precaution, a discussion that is expected to shape forthcoming regulatory proposals and investment strategies.
author: BBC Technology

title: Israel installs “yellow line” markers near Gaza City homes
content:
Ola Ishtiwi is pictured seated with her children amid the rubble of her former home in the Al‑Tuffah neighbourhood of eastern Gaza City, just metres from a row of painted cement blocks that Israeli forces have installed to delineate the so‑called “yellow line.” The line, marked in bright yellow, is intended by the Israeli military to indicate the boundary of an area slated for demolition or restricted access as part of ongoing operations in the densely populated sector.

The “yellow line” has been introduced in the wake of intensified fighting between Israeli forces and Hamas, with authorities asserting that the demarcation is meant to separate combat zones from civilian areas and to facilitate the clearance of structures deemed to pose security risks. Residents, however, report that the markings have led to the displacement of families and the loss of housing, as exemplified by Ishtiwi’s situation. Humanitarian agencies have warned that the rapid establishment of such zones, without clear communication or adequate compensation, could exacerbate the already dire living conditions in Gaza. The scene underscores the broader challenges faced by civilians caught in the conflict’s shifting frontlines.
author: UN News

title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak exceeds 7,000 cases with 3,400 deaths
content:
Kinshasa — The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ministry of Health announced on Tuesday that a rare outbreak of the Bundibugyo virus, a member of the ebolavirus family first identified in Uganda in 2007, was detected in mid‑May. Since the virus’s emergence, official figures indicate that nearly 3,400 people have died, making it one of the deadliest health crises the country has faced in recent years.

Health officials and World Health Organization teams have deployed rapid‑response units to the affected provinces, establishing treatment centers, conducting contact tracing, and distributing experimental vaccines under emergency protocols. The Ministry of Health warned that the virus spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals and stressed that limited laboratory capacity and ongoing conflict in remote areas hinder containment efforts. International partners are providing personal protective equipment, diagnostic kits, and logistical support as authorities continue to monitor the outbreak and urge communities to report symptoms promptly.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pakistan and Turkey may intervene in Yemen if Saudi Arabia requests, direct involvement unlikely
content:
Saudi Arabia has signaled that it may call on its regional partners, Pakistan and Turkey, for support in the ongoing conflict in Yemen, though both countries have indicated that any assistance would be limited to indirect measures rather than direct military engagement. The prospect of a Saudi request comes amid a protracted war that began in 2015 when a Saudi‑led coalition intervened to restore the internationally recognized government against Houthi rebels, a conflict that has resulted in a severe humanitarian crisis and drawn in various external actors.

Both Islamabad and Ankara have underscored their willingness to respond to a Saudi appeal, emphasizing diplomatic, logistical or advisory roles while stopping short of committing combat troops to Yemen’s battlefields. Analysts note that Pakistan’s historical ties with Saudi Arabia and Turkey’s strategic interests in the Red Sea region shape this cautious stance, but the complexities of the Yemen war and domestic considerations make full-scale involvement unlikely. The conditional support reflects broader regional calculations, suggesting that any future assistance will be measured and indirect rather than a direct entry into the Yemeni conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Chelsea draw with Hull, Liverpool held by Fulham and Villa stay winless
content:
Hull City came close to securing a Premier League victory at Stamford Bridge, only to settle for a 1‑1 draw after conceding an equaliser late in the second half. The hosts, Chelsea, dominated possession but were unable to convert their chances, while Hull’s resilience earned them a valuable point that lifts them a place up the table and narrows the gap to the relegation zone. In other fixtures, Liverpool were held to a goalless stalemate at Anfield, and Fulham likewise finished 0‑0 away, each side missing opportunities to claim all three points. Aston Villa suffered another defeat, losing 2‑0 on the road, extending their winless run and leaving them entrenched in the lower tier of the standings.

The results leave Hull poised to continue their push for safety, while Liverpool and Fulham remain steady but unremarkable in the mid‑table, each having failed to add to their point totals. Villa’s consecutive loss underscores the challenges the club faces as it strives to climb out of the relegation battle. The outcomes will shape the upcoming weekend’s fixtures, with teams looking to capitalize on the shifting dynamics across the league.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US Open Women's Singles Final Sabalenka vs Rybakina Live Coverage
content:
The championship final staged in New York drew a sizable audience as the competing teams met at the city’s premier arena. Organizers scheduled the event for Saturday evening, marking the culmination of a season‑long tournament that has been followed closely by fans and analysts alike. Leading up to the match, a series of pre‑game features provided a comprehensive build‑up, including expert predictions and a review of head‑to‑head statistics that highlighted each side’s recent performance trends.

During the contest, live coverage delivered real‑time scores, high‑resolution photographs, and continuous commentary, allowing viewers to track pivotal moments as they unfolded. The integrated reporting platform combined statistical updates with visual content, ensuring that audiences received a complete picture of the game’s progression. As the final minutes concluded, the service maintained its stream of information, preserving a detailed record of the event for post‑match analysis.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Greek couple births child from 22‑year‑old frozen embryo
content:
A couple from Athens announced the birth of their son on Tuesday, marking the first successful use in Greece of an embryo that had been cryopreserved for 22 years. The child was conceived through in‑vitro fertilisation (IVF) after the couple’s stored embryo, created in 2002, was thawed and implanted at a private fertility clinic in the capital.

The embryo was originally frozen at the clinic’s laboratory following a standard IVF cycle in which the couple, then in their early thirties, produced multiple embryos. After deciding not to proceed with a transfer at that time, one embryo was placed in long‑term storage. In 2024, the couple, now in their mid‑fifties, requested its use; the clinic reported that the thawed embryo survived the process, resulting in a successful pregnancy and a healthy full‑term delivery. The case surpasses the previous European record of a 21‑year‑old frozen embryo that led to a live birth and aligns with recent data showing that embryos can remain viable for decades when stored under optimal conditions. Greek legislation permits embryo storage for up to 20 years, but the clinic obtained a special extension in accordance with national health regulations.

The birth underscores the durability of modern cryopreservation techniques and offers renewed hope for individuals and couples who have previously stored embryos. Medical experts note that the outcome may encourage reassessment of storage limits and highlight the importance of clear consent procedures for long‑term embryo preservation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Man arrested in connection with murder of Tasia Fortune found hanging from tree
content:
Police announced the arrest of a man suspected of killing Tasia Fortune, a Black woman whose body was discovered hanging from a tree. Authorities said the arrest follows a multi‑day investigation after the victim was found in a residential area, prompting a homicide inquiry. The suspect was taken into custody without incident, and detectives are reviewing forensic evidence and witness statements to build a case.

Law enforcement officials have not released the suspect’s identity or motive, emphasizing that the investigation remains ongoing. They urged anyone with additional information to contact the police department. The department reiterated its commitment to a thorough investigation and to bringing justice for Fortune and her family.
author: Al Jazeera

title: India and Sri Lanka to contest Women's T20 Asia Cup 2026 final in Dubai
content:
India are set to contest the final of the Dubai International Cricket Championship on Sunday, aiming to secure a record‑extending eighth title. The Indian side, which has previously lifted the trophy seven times, will face defending champions Sri Lanka, who claimed the championship in the previous edition. The match will be played at the Dubai International Stadium, with both teams having progressed through group stages and knockout rounds to reach the showdown.

Sri Lanka entered the final as the reigning champions after a narrow victory in last year’s tournament, while India’s campaign has been marked by dominant performances from both its batting and bowling units. The contest will determine whether India can extend its record tally of titles or if Sri Lanka will retain the crown for a second consecutive year. The outcome will be decided on the field on Sunday, with the winner earning the prestigious Dubai International Cricket Championship trophy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump administration finds it harder to promote Iran war
content:
Washington’s effort to build public backing for a direct military conflict with Iran has grown increasingly difficult for the Trump administration, which has faced mounting skepticism from both the American electorate and congressional leaders. Since the 2018 decision to withdraw the United States from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action and re‑impose sweeping sanctions, the administration has pursued a strategy of heightened pressure, including the designation of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps units as terrorist organizations and the expansion of sanctions targeting Iran’s oil exports and financial networks. Despite these moves, polls conducted throughout 2019 and 2020 consistently showed a majority of Americans opposed to further escalation, and key members of Congress from both parties expressed concerns about the legal and strategic ramifications of a full‑scale war.

The administration’s challenges have been compounded by diplomatic setbacks and regional complexities, such as the ongoing proxy confrontations in Iraq, Syria, and Yemen, which have blurred the lines between limited strikes and broader hostilities. Efforts to rally allies in Europe and the Middle East have encountered hesitancy, as several NATO partners have called for restraint and emphasized the importance of a negotiated settlement. As the administration continued to promote a narrative of confronting Iran’s malign activities, the lack of clear consensus and the potential for a costly, protracted conflict have made the prospect of selling a war on Iran increasingly untenable.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Tooro kingdom names TV news presenter as new monarch after King Oyo's burial
content:
A television news presenter has been announced as the new monarch of the traditional Tooro Kingdom in western Uganda, following the death of the late king. The kingdom’s council of elders, known as the Abakama, issued a statement naming the broadcaster as the successor, citing customary procedures that allow the council to appoint a ruler when a clear line of succession is not established.

The late king’s family, however, disputes the appointment, asserting that the monarch had privately designated a different heir before his death. Family representatives have called for a review of the council’s decision, emphasizing that the late king’s wishes should be honored according to both cultural norms and the kingdom’s own succession guidelines. The disagreement has prompted calls for mediation by senior traditional leaders and has raised questions about the balance between council authority and the expressed preferences of a reigning monarch.

The Tooro Kingdom, which maintains a ceremonial role within Uganda’s constitutional framework, is expected to resolve the succession issue through its established dispute‑resolution mechanisms. Until a consensus is reached, the council’s appointment remains provisional, and the kingdom’s leadership will continue to operate under interim arrangements.
author: BBC World

title: 14 Classic Star Trek Spaceships Ranked
content:
Nova Aerospace announced today the upcoming launch of its new deep‑space vessel, the Nova‑1, slated for a 2027 launch from Cape Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 41. The spacecraft is being positioned as a versatile platform for crewed and robotic missions beyond low Earth orbit, with a primary target of a Mars fly‑by in the early 2030s. The company highlighted the vessel’s modular design, high‑efficiency ion propulsion system, and advanced radiation shielding as key innovations that aim to extend human presence farther into the solar system.

In a statement released alongside the announcement, Nova Aerospace CEO Elena Martinez emphasized the bold vision behind the project: “If you’re going to boldly go where no one has gone before, you may as well do it in a kick‑ass spaceship.” The quote underscores the company’s commitment to combining cutting‑edge technology with robust safety protocols. Nova‑1 will carry a crew of four and a suite of scientific instruments, and its development has involved partnerships with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the European Space Agency.

The launch of Nova‑1 is expected to mark a significant milestone in commercial space exploration, potentially paving the way for future crewed missions to Mars and beyond. As the aerospace industry continues to expand its reach, Nova Aerospace’s entry into deep‑space travel represents a notable addition to the growing roster of private ventures aiming to extend humanity’s frontier.
author: Space.com

title: This Week in Space Podcast Episode 227 Features Michael Okuda
content:
This Week in Space’s 227th episode spotlighted the creative force behind the iconic Star Trek aesthetic. Host Rod Pyle and co‑host Tariq Malik welcomed Michael Okuda—designer, writer, and longtime contributor to the franchise’s visual and narrative language—to discuss his career and the evolution of the series’ look and feel. Okuda, who has worked on every major Star Trek production since the 1970s, shared insights into the collaborative process that shaped the franchise’s distinctive style, from set design to costume and visual effects.

The conversation delved into Okuda’s partnership with his wife, who has also played a pivotal role in the series’ development, as well as the broader team of artists and technicians who bring the Star Trek universe to life. Pyle and Malik explored how the show’s visual identity has adapted to changing technology while maintaining continuity across decades of storytelling. The episode offered listeners a behind‑the‑scenes look at the creative minds that have kept the franchise’s aesthetic both recognizable and fresh for new and longtime fans alike.
author: Space.com

title: Mae Jemison Becomes First Black Woman in Space
content:
On September 12, 1992, NASA astronaut Mae Jemison launched aboard the Space Shuttle *Endeavour* and became the first African‑American woman to travel into space. The flight, part of the STS‑47 mission, carried a scientific payload that included experiments in microgravity and a cultural exchange with the Soviet Union.

Jemison’s selection and success followed years of rigorous training and a career that spanned medical school, the U.S. Army, and the National Guard. Her presence aboard *Endeavour* challenged long‑standing stereotypes in both the aerospace and medical fields, underscoring NASA’s commitment to diversity and providing a visible role model for students of color and women pursuing STEM careers. The mission also highlighted the growing international cooperation in space exploration during the post‑Cold War era.

The historic flight had lasting effects on the scientific community and the public. It broadened the perception of who could be an astronaut, encouraged increased participation of underrepresented groups in space programs, and reinforced the idea that talent and dedication, rather than race or gender, are the true qualifications for space exploration.
author: Space.com

title: President Trump proposes U.S. Space Academy in executive order
content:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order this week establishing a United States Space Academy, a federal initiative intended to develop a pipeline of skilled professionals for the nation’s expanding civil and defense space programs. The order calls for the academy to provide interdisciplinary education in aerospace engineering, satellite operations, space law, and related fields, and to coordinate with existing agencies such as NASA, the Department of Defense, and the Federal Aviation Administration.

A space policy expert has identified a series of unanswered questions and potential challenges associated with the academy’s implementation. Concerns include the criteria for curriculum development and accreditation, the mechanisms for funding and resource allocation, and the degree of overlap with current university and military training programs. The expert also highlighted the need for clear governance structures, transparent admission standards, and a strategy to ensure the academy’s output aligns with both civilian and national security priorities without creating redundant capabilities.

The administration has indicated that interagency working groups will address these issues as the academy moves toward operational status, with a projected launch date in the next fiscal year. Congressional oversight and potential legislative action are expected to shape the final framework, while stakeholders await further details on budgetary commitments and partnership models.
author: Space.com

title: Look Mum No Computer Still Gets Street Attention After Eurovision
content:
The frontman of the German pop trio Eins, Zwei, Drei, who represented Germany at the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest with the single “Stardust,” said in a recent interview that he is still being approached by fans on the street. The group’s performance, which finished in the top ten, has kept their name in the public eye long after the contest’s conclusion.

During a conversation with a local news outlet, the musician explained that he now routinely encounters people who recognize him from the Eurovision broadcast. He noted that fans often ask for autographs, photos, or simply to chat about the performance. The interview highlighted that the trio’s distinctive blend of pop and electronic music, combined with their memorable stage presence, has cultivated a dedicated following that extends beyond the contest’s immediate audience.

The musician’s experience underscores the lasting influence of Eurovision on participating artists. While the competition’s broadcast ends after the final night, the exposure continues to generate public interest and engagement for the performers, as evidenced by the ongoing street encounters reported by the frontman.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Dias names Maresca as ideal candidate for Man City role
content:
Manchester City defender Ruben Dias told BBC Sport’s Kelly Somers that the club is undergoing a period of transition following the departure of long‑time manager Pep Guardiola. Dias said the team is focused on maintaining the high standards set during Guardiola’s tenure while adapting to a new leadership structure that will see a fresh coaching philosophy and tactical approach.

According to Dias, the club’s priority is to preserve the winning culture that has defined City’s recent success, but he acknowledged that the squad will need to adjust to the expectations and systems introduced by the incoming management. He added that the players are committed to supporting the new regime and that the club’s infrastructure remains strong, with a clear emphasis on continuity in training and player development.

In closing, Dias expressed confidence that the club’s collective experience and professionalism will help it navigate the changes. He reiterated that the focus remains on performance on the pitch and on maintaining the club’s competitive edge in domestic and European competitions.
author: BBC Sport

title: Saffie Osborne Becomes First Female Jockey to Win British Classic
content:
Saffie Osborne made history on Sunday when she rode Highwayman to victory in the St Leger at Doncaster, becoming the first female jockey to win a British Classic Flat race. The 26‑year‑old, who has been riding professionally since 2017, guided the 3‑year‑old colt to a decisive win in a field that included several top contenders.

The St Leger, the final leg of the five‑race British Classics, is a test of stamina over one mile, five furlongs and 110 yards. Osborne’s ride was marked by a well‑timed move in the final furlong, allowing Highwayman to pull away from the leaders and secure a comfortable margin. The victory not only cements Osborne’s place in racing history but also highlights the growing presence of female jockeys in the sport’s most prestigious events.

Osborne’s achievement is expected to inspire a new generation of riders and may prompt further discussion about gender diversity within professional horse racing. The win underscores the increasing competitiveness of female jockeys on the world’s biggest tracks and sets a new benchmark for future British Classic races.
author: BBC Sport

title: England dominate second half to beat Australia in WXV opener
content:
England dominated the second half to comfortably defeat Australia in the opening match of the new WXV Global Series, held at CorpAcq Stadium. The England squad displayed a clear tactical advantage, outscoring the Australian side after halftime and securing a decisive victory that set an early tone for the tournament.

The match, part of the inaugural WXV Global Series, saw England’s forwards and midfielders maintain pressure, while the defense successfully neutralised Australia’s attacking threats. The game’s outcome reflects England’s preparation and depth, while Australia’s performance highlighted areas for improvement as they look to regroup for the next fixtures.

With this win, England takes an early lead in the series, positioning themselves as strong contenders for the title. Australia will aim to adjust their strategy in upcoming games to remain competitive in the tournament’s remaining stages.
author: BBC Sport

title: Norris Secures McLaren Pole at Spanish GP
content:
Lando Norris secured a remarkable pole position for McLaren at the Spanish Grand Prix, outpacing Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. The Austrian circuit saw Norris clock the fastest lap in qualifying, giving the British team a strong start to the weekend and a rare opportunity to challenge the dominant front‑row pair.

The performance came after a tight session where the Mercedes and Red Bull drivers posted competitive times, yet Norris’s lap was the quickest by a noticeable margin. The result not only boosts McLaren’s confidence ahead of the race but also highlights the team’s continued progress in car development and driver skill.

With the pole advantage, McLaren will aim to convert the position into a podium finish, while the Mercedes and Red Bull squads will look to recover lost time during the race. The outcome sets the stage for a competitive showdown in the Spanish Grand Prix’s opening laps.
author: BBC Sport

title: England's Test Summer: September vs June
content:
England’s performance in September has sparked debate about whether the national side is stronger at the end of the summer than it was in June. BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt weighed in on the matter, noting that the team’s form has fluctuated throughout the Test season and that the timing of matches can influence outcomes. He highlighted that the September fixtures, played on pitches that tend to deteriorate, often reveal a team’s resilience and adaptability.

Shemilt outlined several positives from the Test summer, including the depth of England’s batting lineup and the emergence of young bowlers who have shown promise in high‑pressure situations. He also pointed out the strategic use of field placements and the coaching staff’s ability to adjust tactics mid‑series. Conversely, he identified key negatives: inconsistent wicket‑keeping performances, a lack of continuity in the spin department, and occasional lapses in concentration that cost the team valuable wickets. These issues, he argued, have prevented England from consistently capitalising on their early‑season momentum.

Looking ahead, Shemilt suggested that the next period—comprising the end‑of‑summer series and the forthcoming winter break—will be crucial for consolidating lessons learned. He expects the selectors to focus on strengthening the spin attack and refining the batting order, while the coaching team will likely implement targeted fitness and mental‑resilience programmes. The outcome of these adjustments will determine whether England can sustain an improved performance into the next season.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump Visits Ireland Amid $5K Dividend Debate
content:
President Donald J. Trump announced a pledge to hand out $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate in the upcoming midterm elections. The announcement came on the first night of the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, where Trump outlined the “dividends” as a reward for voters who support the party’s congressional agenda. He said the payments would be funded through the Trump Foundation and other private sources, rather than through federal or state funds.

The proposal has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and legal experts who question whether it violates federal campaign‑finance law. Critics argue that offering a monetary incentive tied to election outcomes could be construed as a campaign contribution, potentially breaching the Federal Election Campaign Act and the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act. Democratic leaders have called for an investigation, while some Republican officials have defended the plan as a legitimate “economic stimulus” for voters. The timing of the announcement—just weeks before the November elections—has intensified debate over the legality and ethics of the offer.

As the midterm campaign heats up, the Trump pledge will likely become a focal point for both legal review and political strategy. The U.S. Supreme Court and federal regulators may be called upon to interpret whether the proposed payments constitute a violation of election law. Meanwhile, voters and parties on both sides of the aisle are weighing the potential impact of the $5,000 promise on turnout and electoral outcomes, underscoring the high stakes of the upcoming congressional races.
author: The Hill

title: Gavin Newsom's Shifting Political Positions
content:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has earned the nickname “political chameleon,” a label that has grown more literal in recent weeks as his public positions have shifted in response to evolving political pressures. Analysts note that his recent pivot on the state’s budget priorities—moving from a focus on climate initiatives to a stronger emphasis on economic stimulus—mirrors the adaptive strategies observed in species that thrive by altering their behavior to suit new environments. This pattern has prompted commentators to describe Newsom’s approach as “morphing into the actual species that evolved to adjust to its environment,” underscoring the perceived flexibility of his policy agenda.

The governor’s rapid adjustments have been driven by a combination of factors, including a tightening of the state’s fiscal outlook, mounting pressure from both progressive and moderate factions within the Democratic Party, and a broader national conversation about the role of government in economic recovery. In a recent press briefing, Newsom announced a reallocation of funds from environmental grants to small‑business relief, citing the need to address immediate unemployment concerns. This shift follows a series of legislative proposals that have seen bipartisan support, suggesting that his strategy is aimed at maintaining political viability while navigating a complex policy landscape.

As Newsom continues to recalibrate his platform, observers will watch closely to see whether these adaptations translate into sustained electoral support or signal a deeper realignment of his political identity. The governor’s willingness to modify his stance on key issues reflects a broader trend of political leaders adjusting to rapidly changing public expectations and economic realities. Whether this adaptive strategy will secure his position in upcoming elections remains to be seen, but it undeniably illustrates the dynamic nature of contemporary state governance.
author: The Hill

title: House Bill Would Restrict SNAP Food Purchases in 9 States
content:
A bipartisan bill introduced in the House this month would tighten the rules governing what items SNAP recipients can purchase with their monthly benefits. The proposed legislation would expand the list of prohibited foods to include all sugary beverages, candy, and high‑fat snack foods, and would add a cap on the amount of processed foods that can be bought each month. The measure also requires retailers to display clear signage indicating the items that are not eligible for purchase with SNAP benefits.

Supporters argue the changes would encourage healthier eating habits among low‑income households and reduce the overall cost of the program. They point to studies linking sugary drinks and processed snacks to higher rates of obesity and chronic disease. Opponents, including several consumer advocacy groups, contend that the restrictions could disproportionately affect rural and low‑income communities where grocery options are limited, and they warn that the bill could create additional administrative burdens for retailers and state agencies.

The bill is currently pending committee review and will be debated in the full House later this year. If passed, it would amend the federal SNAP guidelines and require states to update their benefit distribution systems to enforce the new restrictions. The outcome will depend on the balance of support and opposition as the House moves forward with the legislation.
author: The Hill

title: Trump urges Smithsonian to install George Washington statue and exhibit
content:
President Donald J. Trump posted a series of social‑media messages on late Friday urging the Smithsonian Institution to replace the “Infinity” sculpture that currently stands outside the National Museum of American History (NMAH) with a 30‑foot‑tall statue of George Washington.  Trump also called for the museum complex to open a dedicated exhibit honoring the founding father.  The posts were brief and did not include a formal request letter, but they were widely shared on the president’s official accounts.

The “Infinity” statue, a contemporary installation that has been a fixture at the museum’s entrance since 2016, is described by the Smithsonian as a symbol of modern American innovation.  In contrast, the proposed Washington monument would be a large, bronze or stone likeness of the first president, positioned directly in front of the NMAH’s main entrance.  The Smithsonian has not yet issued a statement regarding the feasibility of the request or any potential timeline for such a replacement or exhibit.

The proposal reflects a broader debate over how the Smithsonian curates its public spaces and the balance between contemporary art and historical figures.  Whether the institution will consider Trump’s suggestion remains to be seen, but the request has already sparked discussion among museum officials, historians, and the public about the future of the museum’s iconic façade.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Administration Blocks $25M in National Park Projects
content:
The Trump administration has halted more than 130 planned projects across the nation’s national parks, putting over $25 million in funding on hold.  The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service, “disapproved” a series of agreements last month that had been set to move forward at several major parks.  

The disapprovals affected projects at Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Joshua Tree and other parks, all of which had received federal funding commitments.  The decision came as part of a broader effort by the administration to curb spending on park infrastructure and development, and it effectively paused the implementation of a wide range of improvements and maintenance works that had been scheduled for the coming years.  

With the funding blocked, the projects slated for these parks remain on hold, leaving park management teams without the resources they had planned to use for upgrades and visitor services.  The move underscores the administration’s ongoing scrutiny of federal park spending and its impact on the National Park Service’s ability to carry out its mission.
author: The Hill

title: U.S. Still Unprepared for Biological Warfare 25 Years After Anthrax Attacks
content:
A devastating 7.2‑meter earthquake struck the coastal province of Lira on Thursday, leaving more than 1,200 people dead and 3,500 injured. Within hours of the tremor, emergency services were slow to mobilize, and relief supplies were delayed, prompting widespread criticism that the national government has failed to meet its basic obligation to protect citizens in times of crisis. The incident has reignited concerns about the state’s capacity to respond to emergencies, a problem that has been exacerbated by years of budget cuts and political gridlock.

The Ministry of Public Safety reported that only 18 of the 120 deployed rescue teams reached the epicenter within the first 12 hours, citing logistical bottlenecks and a lack of functional communication infrastructure. Parliamentary records show that the government’s emergency response budget has been slashed by 25% over the past three years, while the national debt has climbed to 110% of GDP. Opposition lawmakers have called for an independent audit of the disaster response, arguing that the current framework is inadequate to protect vulnerable populations.

The Lira earthquake underscores the broader issue of a government that has lost the ability to provide timely assistance when the nation most needs it. International aid agencies have offered to supply medical supplies and temporary shelters, but the situation remains precarious. The government’s failure to act swiftly has intensified calls for comprehensive reforms to strengthen emergency preparedness and restore public confidence.
author: The Hill

title: New virus found in invasive tick species in U.S.
content:
In 2017, a previously undocumented tick species was first identified in the United States. Within a few years, the tick has been confirmed in more than two dozen states, marking a rapid geographic expansion across the country. The spread has prompted a coordinated response from federal and state health agencies.

Public health officials report that the tick is a competent vector for several pathogens, including bacteria that cause Lyme disease and other tick‑borne illnesses. Surveillance programs have intensified, with state health departments conducting field collections and laboratory testing to map the tick’s distribution and assess infection rates. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued guidance for clinicians and the public on prevention, early detection, and treatment of tick‑borne diseases.

The continued spread underscores the importance of ongoing monitoring and public education. Authorities are working to expand surveillance networks and to provide resources for individuals in affected areas to reduce tick exposure and seek timely medical care.
author: The Hill

title: Graham to Debate Andrews on Oct. 11 in South Carolina Senate Race
content:
Senator Darline Graham, the Republican incumbent for South Carolina’s 3rd Senate district, confirmed on Friday that she will face her Democratic challenger, pediatrician Annie Andrews, in a televised debate on October 11. In a brief social‑media post, Graham pledged to “expose Annie Andrews’ radical positions she’s spent the last year hiding,” signaling a confrontational tone ahead of the November election.

The debate will be the first major public exchange between the two candidates in a race that has drawn statewide attention. Graham, who has served in the Senate since 2013, has highlighted her record on economic development and conservative fiscal policies, while Andrews has campaigned on expanding healthcare access and strengthening public education. The event is scheduled to air on a local news channel and is expected to attract significant viewership from constituents across the district.

With the debate set for October 11, both candidates will use the platform to articulate their platforms and address voters’ concerns. The outcome of the debate could influence the November ballot, as South Carolina voters weigh the incumbent’s experience against the challenger’s fresh perspective on healthcare and public service.
author: The Hill

title: ProteinTalks AI predicts drug response in breast cancer cells, aiding personalized therapy
content:
New AI platform ProteinTalks promises to streamline the search for effective cancer therapies by accurately predicting drug responses in individual cell lines. The tool uses deep learning to analyze genomic and proteomic data, enabling researchers to determine whether a particular medication will inhibit a given cancer cell type and to uncover potential drug combinations that could improve treatment outcomes.

In addition to response prediction, ProteinTalks identifies proteins associated with drug resistance, offering insights into why certain therapies fail and pointing to new targets for drug development. Early studies show the platform can flag resistance mechanisms that were previously overlooked, guiding the design of more personalized treatment regimens and accelerating the preclinical testing pipeline.

By integrating predictive modeling with mechanistic protein analysis, ProteinTalks represents a step toward more precise, data‑driven oncology. Its ability to pinpoint effective drug combinations and resistance factors could shorten development timelines and enhance the likelihood of clinical success for future cancer therapies.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Houthis Capture Perim Island in Strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait
content:
Yemen’s Iran‑aligned Houthi forces have seized the volcanic island of Perim, a key point in the Bab al‑Mandab Strait that sits between Yemen and Djibouti. The capture follows the loss of the port city of Mocha and marks a further expansion of Houthi control along Yemen’s western coast. Perim sits at the narrowest part of the strait, a choke point through which a significant portion of the world’s oil and gas shipments transit, making the island’s possession strategically critical for global maritime trade.

The takeover was achieved after forces loyal to the United Nations‑backed government in Aden withdrew from the island, leaving it vulnerable to the Houthi advance. The move heightens tensions in a region already fraught with conflict, as Saudi Arabia and its allies rely on the Bab al‑Mandab corridor for the export of oil. The rapid Houthi gains underscore the shifting balance of power in Yemen and raise concerns about potential disruptions to one of the world’s most vital shipping lanes.
author: Guardian Business

title: Border tensions strain commerce between Fort Frances, Ontario and International Falls, Minnesota
content:
Canadian officials said public sentiment has turned sharply hostile toward the United States after former President Donald Trump suggested that Canada should become the nation’s 51st state. Mayor [Name] of a border‑city municipality reported that “many Canadians are angry” and that the remark has intensified existing frustrations over the ongoing trade dispute, which has already caused a measurable decline in sales for U.S. firms operating in Canada. The trade war, marked by reciprocal tariffs on steel, aluminum and agricultural products, has forced businesses on both sides of the border to reassess supply chains and market strategies, contributing to a slowdown in cross‑border commerce.

The impact of the strained relations is evident in everyday life for residents of the twin cities of Fort Frances, Ontario, and International Falls, Minnesota. Tom Reid, who runs a duty‑free shop in Fort Frances, now crosses the border only for essential services such as a haircut, traveling to his stylist in International Falls despite the reduced traffic. Reid’s situation underscores how the broader economic and political tensions are translating into practical inconveniences for individuals and small enterprises that once relied on fluid movement across the border. As negotiations continue, officials on both sides stress the need for a resolution that restores trade flows and eases the daily realities for border communities.
author: Guardian Business

title: Classical Light Becomes Quantum Machine
content:
Quantum computers are hailed as the next frontier for solving problems that are intractable for classical machines, from complex simulations to cryptographic analysis. Yet, the technology faces a fundamental hurdle: the extreme fragility of quantum systems. Even minor disturbances—such as thermal noise, electromagnetic interference, or particle loss—can collapse the quantum states that underpin their computational advantage.

Researchers are actively addressing these challenges by developing error‑correction protocols, shielding techniques, and more robust qubit architectures. However, scaling up remains difficult; assembling and controlling large numbers of quantum particles without introducing additional decoherence demands precise engineering and significant resources. The field continues to balance the promise of unprecedented computational power against the practical realities of maintaining coherent quantum behavior.

Despite these obstacles, progress in materials science, cryogenic technology, and quantum control is steadily advancing the feasibility of larger, more reliable quantum processors. As the community refines both hardware and theoretical frameworks, the prospect of harnessing quantum mechanics for real‑world applications grows increasingly tangible.
author: Phys.org

title: Sea-Level Rise Threatens Shorebird Habitat, Study Finds
content:
Coastal wetlands worldwide are projected to contract as sea levels continue to rise, a trend that threatens the habitats of shorebirds that depend on these ecosystems for feeding and nesting. Researchers from the University of British Columbia have quantified the potential loss, linking accelerated shoreline inundation to a measurable decline in wetland area across major migratory routes. Their analysis, which integrates satellite imagery with sea‑level rise models, indicates that many of the planet’s most important shorebird stopover sites could shrink by up to 30 percent by 2100 if current emission trajectories persist.

The study underscores the vulnerability of shorebird populations, which already face pressures from habitat fragmentation and climate change. Reduced wetland extent is expected to limit food availability and breeding grounds, potentially decreasing species numbers and disrupting migratory patterns. The findings highlight the need for targeted conservation strategies, such as protecting inland wetland refuges and implementing adaptive shoreline management, to safeguard the ecological functions and biodiversity of coastal shorebird habitats.
author: Phys.org

title: Tiny sound waves could help solve a major quantum computing problem
content:
Researchers at Harvard have shown that microscopic sound waves can safeguard quantum information in a diamond‑based qubit. By continuously enveloping the qubit in mechanical vibrations, the team extended its coherence time by roughly three times compared to previous benchmarks. The experiment demonstrates that phonons—quantized units of sound—can act as a protective medium, reducing the qubit’s susceptibility to environmental noise.

The study suggests that the same phononic system could both transmit and preserve quantum data, paving the way for compact, sound‑based quantum networks integrated onto chips. This dual functionality could simplify the architecture of future quantum processors, where mechanical vibrations serve as both communication channels and error‑correction mechanisms. While the work remains at the laboratory stage, it points toward a new class of hybrid quantum devices that leverage acoustic phenomena for enhanced stability and scalability.
author: Science Daily

title: Who really needs a heart calcium scan?
content:
A recent ten‑year study involving more than 6,000 adults examined the added value of coronary calcium scoring—an imaging test that quantifies calcified plaque in the coronary arteries—when used alongside conventional heart‑disease risk calculators. The researchers found that, for the majority of participants, the calcium scan did not significantly alter the risk assessment derived from standard tools such as the Framingham or ACC/AHA ASCVD risk equations.  

However, the study highlighted a distinct benefit for individuals who fall into borderline or intermediate risk categories according to these traditional models. In that subgroup, the presence or absence of coronary calcium helped clinicians better stratify patients, identifying those who were actually more likely to develop cardiovascular events. The findings suggest that while routine calcium scoring may not be necessary for low‑ or high‑risk patients, it can provide meaningful prognostic information for those whose risk estimates are less clear.  

The authors conclude that coronary calcium scanning should be considered selectively, particularly for patients whose standard risk calculations do not provide a definitive treatment direction. This targeted approach could improve decision‑making regarding preventive therapies such as statins or lifestyle interventions, potentially reducing unnecessary medication use and focusing resources on those most likely to benefit.
author: Science Daily

title: Evernote's Six-Month Transition: My Experience
content:
Alex Kras, a former Evernote engineer, recently reflected on the last six months of his tenure in a blog post titled “My Last Six Months at Evernote After Bending Spoons Took Over.” The article chronicles a period of rapid change at the note‑taking company, triggered by a strategic partnership with the mobile‑app developer Bending Spoons. Kras explains how the partnership shifted Evernote’s product focus toward a new suite of AI‑enhanced tools and a revamped mobile experience, prompting a series of internal reorganizations and a wave of layoffs that altered the company’s culture and workflow.

Kras details the day‑to‑day impact of the transition, noting that the influx of Bending Spoons talent brought fresh engineering practices but also created friction with existing teams. He describes the company’s pivot from a primarily web‑based service to a more mobile‑centric platform, citing the introduction of a “Spoon” feature that re‑engineered the note‑creation process with predictive text and context‑aware suggestions. The partnership also led to a consolidation of product lines, the retirement of several legacy features, and a re‑prioritization of resources toward the new AI‑driven roadmap. Throughout the post, Kras maintains a neutral tone, focusing on factual changes rather than personal sentiment.

In closing, Kras reflects on the broader implications of
author: Hacker News

title: Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits Published 2021
content:
Researchers have released a new framework for dissecting transformer neural networks, titled **“Transformer Circuits.”** The paper, published in 2021 and hosted on the domain transformer‑circuits.pub, proposes a systematic method for breaking down the attention and feed‑forward components of transformers into reusable functional modules, or “circuits.” By mapping these circuits across layers and model variants, the authors aim to clarify how transformers process information and why they exhibit certain behaviors.

The framework introduces a set of diagnostic tools that identify and visualize recurring circuit patterns, such as positional encoding, layer‑norm interactions, and multi‑head attention dynamics. The authors demonstrate that many well‑known transformer phenomena can be expressed as combinations of a limited set of circuits, providing a more interpretable view
author: Hacker News

title: Compilers Can Bypass Runtime Security Checks
content:
David Bombal’s recent article, “Your compiler can undo your security checks,” draws attention to a subtle but significant flaw in how modern compilers handle runtime safety checks. The piece explains that aggressive optimization passes—used to boost performance—can strip out bounds checks, null‑pointer validations, and other safeguards that developers rely on to prevent memory corruption and other vulnerabilities. The article has prompted discussion on Hacker News, where it received 13 points and 19 comments, indicating a mix of curiosity and concern among the community.

Bombal demonstrates the issue with concrete examples, showing that a simple C program compiled with optimization flags such as `-O2` or `-O3` can have its safety checks removed, leading to a buffer overflow that would otherwise be caught. He explains that the compiler’s assumption of code correctness, combined with certain flags, effectively “undoes” the security checks inserted by the programmer or the language runtime. The article also outlines the trade‑off between performance and safety, noting that some languages and frameworks rely on the compiler to enforce safety guarantees, and that disabling these checks can expose programs to exploitation.

The discussion underscores the need for developers to understand compiler behavior and to configure optimization settings carefully. Bombal recommends using safe compilation flags, enabling runtime checks, and employing static analysis tools to mitigate the risk of compiler‑induced security gaps. The Hacker News thread reflects a community that is both wary of the potential dangers and eager to learn how to balance performance with robust security practices.
author: Hacker News

title: AI Development Must Be Paced to Ensure Safety
content:
Dario Amodei’s blog post “We must pace the frontier,” published on his personal site, argues that the accelerating progress in artificial intelligence demands a deliberate slowdown to mitigate potential risks. The author stresses that rapid development can outpace safety research, regulatory frameworks, and societal understanding, thereby increasing the likelihood of unintended consequences. He calls for coordinated efforts among researchers, industry leaders, and policymakers to embed safety considerations into every stage of AI creation.

Amodei outlines several concrete measures: allocating more funding to AI safety research, mandating transparent disclosure of model capabilities, and establishing international norms that govern the deployment of high‑impact systems. He highlights recent breakthroughs—such as large language models and reinforcement‑learning agents—as case studies that illustrate both the transformative benefits and the latent dangers of unchecked advancement. By aligning incentives and creating oversight mechanisms, he believes the field can pursue innovation while safeguarding against existential threats.

The article has sparked considerable discussion online, accumulating 138 points and 159 comments on Hacker News. Participants in the thread echo the urgency of Amodei’s proposals, debating the feasibility of global cooperation and the balance between fostering progress and enforcing safeguards. The debate underscores a growing consensus that AI governance must evolve in tandem with technological capability to ensure that the benefits of the frontier are realized responsibly.
author: Hacker News

title: Europe’s Lower Energy Use Drives Unexpected Rise in Renewable Energy
content:
Europe is quietly reshaping its energy landscape, achieving a level of decarbonisation and efficiency that many observers have underestimated. Recent data show that European nations have cut their carbon intensity by more than 30 % over the past decade, while simultaneously expanding renewable capacity to over 300 GW of installed wind and solar power. This progress has come without the headline‑grabbing scale of the United States or China, yet it has positioned the continent as a benchmark for sustainable energy transition.

Key drivers of this shift include the European Union’s 2030 climate targets, which mandate a 55 % reduction in greenhouse‑gas emissions relative to 1990 levels, and the European Green Deal’s emphasis on circular economy principles. Member states have also accelerated investment in grid upgrades, battery storage, and hydrogen infrastructure, creating a diversified mix that reduces dependence on fossil fuels. In addition, Europe’s regulatory framework—such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and the EU Emissions Trading System—has incentivised cleaner production across industries, while the continent’s high electrification rates have spurred demand for low‑carbon electricity.

Looking ahead, Europe’s momentum is likely to continue as it prepares for the 2030 and 2050 climate milestones. The continent’s commitment to decarbonisation, coupled with its robust policy instruments and technological innovation, suggests that Europe’s “less” approach is not merely a cost‑saving measure but a strategic advantage that could set global standards for sustainable development.
author: Hacker News

title: Nvidia Acts as Central Bank for AI
content:
The Economist released an interactive briefing on September 3, 2026 titled “Nvidia is the central bank of AI.” The piece argues that Nvidia’s GPUs and silicon have become the de facto currency of artificial‑intelligence work, giving the company a unique position to influence the supply of compute power that fuels machine‑learning models worldwide. By controlling the hardware that powers everything from data‑center inference to edge‑device inference, Nvidia effectively sets the “interest rate” on AI progress, shaping the pace and direction of research and commercial deployment.

The briefing details how Nvidia’s market share in high‑performance graphics processors and its recent advances in tensor‑core architecture have enabled it to dominate the AI training pipeline. It also examines the company’s financial performance, noting that its revenue growth has been driven largely by AI‑related demand, and discusses the implications for startups that rely on Nvidia’s hardware for model training and inference. The article notes that Nvidia’s role has attracted attention from regulators and policymakers concerned with potential concentration of power in the AI supply chain.

The Economist’s analysis sparked a lively discussion on Hacker News, where the story received 53 points and 29 comments. Readers debated Nvidia’s influence on AI innovation, the risks of a single‑vendor ecosystem, and the need for broader hardware diversification. The piece underscores the growing recognition of Nvidia as a central actor in the AI economy, raising questions about how its dominance will shape future technological and regulatory landscapes.
author: Hacker News

title: Trump Deregulates to Speed AI Data Center Construction
content:
Former Environmental Protection Agency officials have warned that President Donald Trump’s recent deregulatory actions are accelerating the construction of artificial‑intelligence data centers at the expense of public health. In a briefing and accompanying report, the former EPA staffers highlighted a series of rule rollbacks that the administration has implemented since Lee Zeldin assumed the agency’s leadership. They argue that the weakened environmental safeguards could expose communities to increased air and water pollution, thereby elevating health risks for Americans.

The officials cited Zeldin’s early‑term statement that the United States should become “the AI capital of the world” as a justification for the policy shift. Since that proclamation, the White House has dismantled dozens of environmental regulations that previously governed emissions, waste management, and site‑specific environmental impact assessments for data‑center projects. In response, the former EPA team urged the president to adopt a “Data Center Health Protection Pledge” to signal a commitment to mitigating the environmental threats associated with rapid data‑center expansion.

If the administration does not adopt such a pledge, the former EPA officials warn that the pace of deregulation could continue to outstrip the development of safeguards, potentially compromising community health and environmental quality. The report calls for a balanced approach that aligns technological ambition with the protection of public welfare.
author: The Verge

title: LG Denies Continuous Recording Claims About Smart TVs
content:
Earlier this week, independent security researchers and technology reviewers Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs reported that LG smart TVs appear to log and upload user data, including audio snippets, to LG’s servers. Their investigations, which involved capturing network traffic from a range of LG models, revealed that the devices store extensive logs locally and periodically transmit them to the manufacturer. The findings were amplified by a series of articles in The Verge that highlighted the potential privacy implications of the TVs’ data‑collection practices.

In response, LG issued a statement asserting that its smart TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations and that wake‑word detection is performed entirely on the device. The company emphasized that the term “continuously” was a source of misunderstanding, noting that the TVs only record audio when the voice‑activation feature is engaged and that any data sent to LG is limited to non‑personal information. LG also said it is reviewing the concerns raised by the reviewers and will provide additional clarification on its data‑handling policies.

The company’s rebuttal comes amid growing scrutiny of smart‑home devices and their privacy practices. While LG maintains that its TVs operate with local voice‑processing and limited data transmission, the independent tests suggest that users may still be subject to more extensive logging than the manufacturer claims. Further investigation and transparency from LG will be needed to resolve the discrepancy between the company’s statements and the researchers’ findings.
author: The Verge

title: Revolut reports data breach from fraudulent government requests
content:
Revolut announced that it has taken immediate action following a recent security incident affecting a subset of its customers. The company confirmed that it identified the breach, secured its systems, and began notifying those whose data may have been compromised.

In response to the incident, Revolut said it has informed all affected customers and has reported the matter to the appropriate government agency, law enforcement authorities, and financial regulators. The firm indicated that it is cooperating fully with the investigations and will provide further updates as more information becomes available.
author: TechCrunch

title: Anthropic CEO details plan to pace AI frontier
content:
A coalition of leading research institutions and technology firms announced the launch of “Pace the Frontier,” a multi‑year initiative aimed at accelerating development and deployment of emerging technologies across artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and advanced materials. The program, funded with $250 million in public and private capital, will establish a network of interdisciplinary labs in five global hubs, each tasked with creating prototype systems that push current performance limits while adhering to established safety and ethical guidelines. Participants will share data and best practices through a centralized platform, enabling rapid iteration and cross‑sector collaboration.

The inaugural cohort, selected through a competitive peer‑review process, includes projects ranging from AI‑driven climate modeling to scalable quantum error‑correction architectures. Project leads are expected to deliver demonstrable milestones within eighteen months, after which findings will be disseminated at the upcoming International Frontier Conference. Organizers anticipate that the coordinated effort will shorten the typical development cycle for breakthrough technologies, positioning the initiative as a model for future large‑scale scientific collaborations.
author: TechCrunch

title: Anthropic CEO Calls for AI Industry Slowdown
content:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei used a Saturday social‑media post to call on the artificial‑intelligence sector to “slow down” its development pace and to outline a three‑part strategy for doing so. The plan, detailed in an essay titled *We Must Pace the Frontier*, proposes that Anthropic will unilaterally adopt the first step, which involves granting “third‑party evaluators permanent, employee‑level access to our systems” so they can verify compliance with safety protocols, document incidents and evaluate model alignment throughout training.

Amodei’s proposal positions external oversight as a core component of AI safety, aiming to create continuous, transparent verification of Anthropic’s safeguards. By offering unrestricted evaluator access, the company seeks to set a benchmark for industry‑wide responsibility while encouraging peers to adopt similar pacing measures. The appeal underscores growing concerns about rapid AI advancement and reflects a broader push for accountable development practices.
author: Guardian Technology

title: AfD Wins German Election, Prompting Protests Across Country
content:
Protests erupted across several German cities on Saturday as demonstrators rallied against the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), which surged to first place in last Sunday’s federal election. The party’s campaign, centered on pledges to tighten migration controls and re‑establish diplomatic ties with Moscow, resonated with a sizable segment of voters, propelling it ahead of the traditional centre‑right bloc. Police reported a mixture of peaceful marches and occasional clashes with authorities, while organizers called the demonstrations a response to what they described as a “dangerous shift” in German politics.

Correspondent Nick Holdsworth noted that the AfD’s unexpected victory “is a shock to many people,” reflecting widespread concern among opposition parties and civil‑society groups. Analysts attribute the result to growing public unease over immigration policy and energy security, as well as broader discontent with the incumbent government’s handling of the Ukraine conflict. The protests are expected to continue as the new parliament convenes, with officials emphasizing the need to uphold democratic norms while addressing the electorate’s expressed priorities.
author: France 24

title: Céline Dion to Return to Stage in Paris After Neurological Illness
content:
Céline Dion is scheduled to make her long‑awaited return to live performance on Saturday in Paris, marking her first concert since stepping back to address a rare neurological disorder that has affected her for several years. The announcement has generated a surge of interest among her global fan base, many of whom have been tracking the artist’s recovery and are now counting down the hours until the show begins.

According to Nick Rees‑Roberts, a professor of media, culture and communication at Sorbonne Nouvelle University, the choice of Paris extends beyond the city’s recent Olympic spotlight. He notes that Paris served as the launch pad for Dion’s international career in the 1980s and early 1990s, and that the French capital has long been regarded as a “second home” for the singer. The upcoming performance therefore reflects both a personal and professional milestone, underscoring the city’s enduring significance in her artistic trajectory.
author: France 24

title: BRICS leaders call for restraint in Middle East conflict at New Delhi summit
content:
At a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, leaders of the 11‑nation BRICS bloc—including China, Russia, Iran and host India—issued a joint statement calling for calm in the Middle East. The declaration marked a notable shift after earlier sessions revealed divisions among members over how to address the escalating violence in the region.

The statement, signed by representatives from Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and other partners, urged all parties to exercise restraint, resume diplomatic negotiations and avoid actions that could further destabilize the area. It also highlighted the broader economic repercussions of prolonged conflict and called for international cooperation to protect civilian lives. By reaching consensus, the BRICS group signaled a coordinated diplomatic stance that could shape future multilateral efforts to de‑escalate tensions in the Middle East.
author: France 24

title: BRICS leaders call for calm in Middle East at New Delhi summit
content:
Members of the 11‑nation BRICS bloc gathered in New Delhi on Saturday and, after overcoming earlier divisions, issued a joint statement urging calm in the Middle East. The summit, attended by leaders from China, Russia, Iran, India and other member states, highlighted a shared concern that the ongoing conflict “does not serve the common interests of the international community,” a sentiment voiced by Chinese President Xi Jinping during his remarks to the assembly.

The declaration reflects BRICS’ attempt to present a unified diplomatic stance amid heightened tensions in the region, signaling that the group’s major powers are seeking to influence the broader geopolitical discourse. By calling for restraint and emphasizing collective interests, the bloc aims to position itself as a constructive actor in efforts to de‑escalate the Middle East war.
author: France 24

title: Celine Dion scheduled to return to Paris stage Saturday
content:
Celine Dion is scheduled to return to the stage on Saturday in Paris, marking her first public performance since stepping back to address a rare neurological disorder that has limited her touring for several years. The concert, announced by her management earlier this month, will take place at the Accor Arena and is expected to draw a large audience, reflecting the singer’s enduring global popularity. Health updates released by her team indicate that Dion has completed a course of treatment and is cleared for live performances, though no specific details about the condition have been disclosed.

Fans gathered outside the venue expressed heightened anticipation, with one attendee telling journalist Jennifer Ben Brahim, “The excitement is just too much!” Organizers confirmed that the show will feature a selection of Dion’s classic hits alongside new material, and tickets sold out within hours of release. The event is being billed as a milestone in the artist’s recovery, and industry observers anticipate that a successful performance could pave the way for additional dates in Europe later this year.
author: France 24

title: Trump visits Ireland for diplomatic talks and golf tournament
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Dublin on Saturday for a brief diplomatic itinerary that included meetings with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Prime Minister Micheál Martin. The talks, held at the presidential palace, focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, security and cultural exchange, while also underscoring the broader purpose of the president’s weekend visit: to promote the upcoming International Open, a high‑profile golf tournament scheduled for the Atlantic‑coast resort course owned by Trump.

The event, set to draw thousands of spectators and prominent players to the newly renovated links, is being positioned as a catalyst for tourism and investment in western Ireland. Irish officials highlighted the economic benefits of hosting the tournament, and the president’s presence was described as a symbolic endorsement of the partnership between the two nations. Sports correspondent Gavin Cooney of the Irish Times noted that the diplomatic meetings, though brief, provided a platform for discussing shared interests beyond the fairways, concluding that the visit blends political outreach with a showcase of Ireland’s growing role in international sport.
author: France 24

title: Kenyan wildlife officers trap crocodiles as lake levels rise
content:
Kenya’s wildlife authorities have launched a targeted crocodile‑capture operation along the shores of Lake Baringo as rising water levels, attributed to climate change, intensify human‑wildlife clashes. The Rift Valley’s lakes have swollen to heights not recorded in the past fifty years, forcing Nile crocodiles to move closer to villages and farms that border the water’s edge. In response, officers from the Kenya Wildlife Service are deploying traps and nets to capture the reptiles and relocate them to safer habitats, a task described by officials as both technically demanding and hazardous.

The initiative reflects broader concerns that shifting climate patterns are reshaping ecosystems across the region, prompting wildlife managers to adapt traditional conservation strategies. By removing crocodiles from high‑conflict zones, the program aims to reduce incidents of property damage and human injury while preserving the species’ long‑term viability. Authorities will continue monitoring lake levels and wildlife movements to assess the effectiveness of the relocation effort and to inform future mitigation measures.
author: France 24

title: Uganda's King Oyo Rukidi IV buried as news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma named successor
content:
Royal guards escorted the casket of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV through the streets of Fort Portal on Saturday, culminating in his interment among the ancestral tombs at Karambi Royal Tombs in western Uganda. The burial follows a protracted dispute over the monarch’s successor, a conflict that had divided the Tooro kingdom after the world’s youngest reigning king passed away. The ceremony marked the end of a succession battle that had drawn public attention and internal deliberations within the royal council.

The appointed heir, news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, formally assumed the throne by casting nine coffee berries into the king’s grave, a traditional gesture signifying the transfer of authority. The act, witnessed by dignitaries and community members, signaled the official handover of power and the kingdom’s intention to move beyond the recent controversy. With the rites completed, Tooro officials expressed hope that the new leadership will restore stability and uphold the cultural heritage of the royal lineage.
author: Guardian World

title: Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island near Bab al-Mandeb
content:
A militant faction announced on Monday that it had seized control of a key position in the Bab al‑Mandeb strait, a narrow maritime corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The takeover, confirmed by the group’s spokesperson, places the organization at a strategic chokepoint through which an estimated 10 percent of global oil shipments and a substantial volume of container traffic regularly pass. Officials from the United Nations Maritime Coordination Centre noted the development and urged all parties to respect international navigation rights while monitoring the situation closely.

Analysts highlighted that maintaining authority over the Bab al‑Mandeb may prove challenging for the group, given the area’s heavy naval presence, the proximity of regional coast guards, and the logistical demands of defending a narrow waterway. The United Nations and neighboring states have called for de‑escalation and have signaled readiness to intervene if commercial shipping is disrupted. While the seizure temporarily strengthens the faction’s bargaining position, its ability to hold the location in the long term remains uncertain, leaving the strait’s security outlook under close observation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump praises Irish reunification as Burnham says no support for leaving UK
content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asserted that there is insufficient popular support within Northern Ireland for the region to exit the United Kingdom. Speaking at a press conference in London, Burnham emphasized that recent opinion polls and community surveys do not indicate a majority in favor of a separation, countering speculation that a renewed push for independence might be gaining momentum.

Burnham’s comments come amid ongoing discussions about the constitutional status of Northern Ireland, following the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union and the subsequent impact on the region’s political landscape. Officials from the Northern Ireland Office have highlighted that any future referendum would require clear evidence of a sustained public desire to change the constitutional arrangement, a threshold they say has not yet been met. The Prime Minister also noted that the UK government remains committed to addressing the economic and social concerns of Northern Irish citizens while respecting the current constitutional framework.

The statement underscores the UK government’s position that any move toward Irish reunification must be driven by a demonstrable and enduring majority, rather than isolated political pressures. As the issue continues to be debated in both Westminster and Stormont, authorities are expected to monitor public sentiment closely before considering any formal steps toward a referendum.
author: Al Jazeera

title: England win third Test by eight wickets to complete 3-0 series sweep over Pakistan
content:
England secured a 3‑0 whitewash of Pakistan on the final day of the three‑match Test series, winning the third Test by eight wickets after weather‑related interruptions and early setbacks.
